Neonates of the St. Croix anole hatch at a snout-to-vent length of 2.0 centimeters [Lb = 2.0 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the energetic constraints of lecithotrophic development within the parchment-shelled egg. Field surveys indicate that egg-laying females deposit clutches during the wet season, and incubation under natural thermal regimes proceeds at an average temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. At this temperature, the interval from oviposition to hatching, or age at birth, is approximately 50 days [ab = approximately 50 days] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Newly emerged hatchlings have a wet weight at birth of just 0.26 grams [Wwb = 0.26 grams], placing them among the lighter-bodied anoline neonates. This initial mass is critical for juvenile survival, as it must sustain the individual through the period of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, when the young anole begins actively foraging for small arthropods in the leaf litter.

Sexual maturation in Anolis acutus is tightly linked to body size rather than chronological age alone. Females undergo puberty and begin reproductive activity once they attain a snout-to-vent length of 3.9 centimeters [Lp = 3.9 centimeters]. This size threshold corresponds to the point at which gonadal activation occurs, triggering gametogenesis and the production of the first egg clutch. In contrast, ultimate body size is strongly dimorphic: females reach a maximum snout-to-vent length of 4.4 centimeters [Li = 4.4 centimeters], whereas males continue growing to a substantially larger ultimate snout-to-vent length of 6.3 centimeters [Li = 6.3 centimeters]. This divergence in asymptotic length is a common pattern among Caribbean anoles and is generally attributed to sexual selection on male body size for territory defense. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 3.05 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.05 grams], a figure consistent with allometric scaling relationships observed in related species.

Reproductive output in the St. Croix anole is constrained by both body size and thermal environment. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females have been recorded producing eggs at a maximum rate that corresponds to approximately 18 eggs over the course of a year. This annual total emerges from a combination of clutch size and laying frequency: gravid females typically deposit a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], and under optimal conditions they can produce as many as 18 clutches annually [F_R_i = 18 clutches annually]. The extended period required for egg formation at this temperature reflects the metabolic limitations of a small-bodied ectotherm. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that Anolis acutus has a relatively moderate reproductive rate for its body size class, likely shaped by the seasonal rainfall patterns of the St. Croix dry forest.

Longevity in this population has been inferred from mark-recapture studies conducted over multiple field seasons. At a mean ambient temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for Anolis acutus in natural habitats is approximately 7 years [am = approximately 7 years], though most individuals are thought to survive for considerably shorter durations due to predation pressure and resource limitation. This lifespan is moderate among small Caribbean anoles, reflecting the trade-off between early reproduction and the accumulation of somatic damage over time. Older individuals, particularly males, exhibit signs of reproductive senescence and a decrease in territorial activity. The relatively slow pace of life suggested by this longevity figure is consistent with the species' moderate growth rates and the extended incubation period of its eggs. Documenting such demographic parameters is essential for understanding the population dynamics of this endemic island species.

To place the life history of Anolis acutus in a broader comparative context, it is instructive to examine its morphological and reproductive traits alongside those of other members of the Anolis genus. The adult female ultimate wet weight of 3.05 grams [Wwi = 3.05 grams] is modest compared to that of larger-bodied Hispaniolan anoles, but the male ultimate wet weight of 7.44 grams [Wwi = 7.44 grams] reveals a pronounced sexual size dimorphism that is among the more extreme recorded for the genus. This dimorphism likely plays a role in the species' mating system, where larger males dominate access to territories and females. Furthermore, the size at female puberty of 3.9 centimeters [Lp = 3.9 centimeters] indicates that females begin reproducing at over 88 percent of their ultimate snout-to-vent length, a pattern characteristic of species with determinate growth. Continued field monitoring of this population will be essential to assess how shifting thermal regimes may alter the onset of breeding and the overall reproductive output of this endemic Caribbean lizard.
